name: Rhinophyma laser / surgery

lead: Rhinophyma is an advanced form of rosacea in which the skin of the lower nose thickens and enlarges into a bulbous, lumpy shape. Treatment of established cases removes or reshapes the excess tissue so the nose regains a smoother, slimmer contour, visible after healing.

It is a recognised clinical procedure that appearance communities mention among nose-related options, not a looksmaxxing invention. Its medical literature is far older than the community, with a preliminary report on CO2 laser removal published in 1980.

paras: Surgeons remove or reshape the excess tissue with a scalpel, electrosurgery, dermabrasion or an ablative carbon dioxide laser, layer by layer, and the nose heals over. The condition involves overgrowth of oil glands and fibrous tissue, and rosacea itself is managed separately with topical or oral medicines.

Reviews describe scarring, pigment change, bleeding and recurrence as general concerns of resurfacing or excision. A biopsy is advised because basal cell carcinoma and other conditions can resemble or hide within rhinophyma. Procedures are performed by physicians and are prescription-level care.

angle.text: Rhinophyma laser or surgical shaving removes the thickened tissue of advanced rosacea to restore a normal nose contour, with the change visible after healing. It is a recognised medical procedure that appearance communities mention, not a looksmaxxing invention.

lead: Rhinophyma laser or surgical treatment is the medical removal of excess tissue from a thickened, bulbous nose caused by advanced rosacea. People seek it to bring the nose back to a smoother, more proportionate contour and, in some cases, to open a nasal airway narrowed by the overgrowth. The usual tools are a sharp blade, electrosurgery, dermabrasion or an ablative carbon dioxide laser, often used in combination [1][2][3].

Rhinophyma itself is a condition in which the skin of the lower nose thickens through enlargement of sebaceous glands and fibrous change. It is regarded as the end stage of the phymatous form of rosacea and is most common in older men of European ancestry [1][2][4]. Popular names include "whiskey nose" and "gin blossom", although a causal link with alcohol has not been established [1][2]. After the tissue is reduced, the area is left to re-epithelialise from the deeper glandular remnants, and the nose can heal with a visibly refined shape [2][3].

The published treatment literature is mostly retrospective: a 1980 four-patient preliminary report on CO2 laser removal, a 2009 review of 124 laser-treated patients in which 118 had good to excellent results at three months, and a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of 149 reports covering 2,720 patients, in which 94 percent of pooled reports described clinical and cosmetic improvement [5][6][6].

The procedure is a recognised clinical treatment rather than a looksmaxxing invention, and it appears in the wiki because it is one of the nose-focused procedures people encounter when researching appearance surgery. Reviews describe the range of surgical and non-surgical options [3][7][6].

sections.h: Terminology and history of the condition
paras: Wikipedia notes that phyma is Greek for swelling or mass, giving the phymatous subtype of rosacea its name, which can also affect the chin, forehead, cheeks, eyelids and ears [4]. Colloquial names include "whiskey nose", "gin blossom", "toros nose" and "potato nose" [1].

Rosacea itself has a long history in the record; Wikipedia says it was possibly described by Theocritus in the third century BC and appears in Chaucer's Canterbury Tales in the 1300s [4]. Rhinophyma was well known before modern treatment: the financier J. P. Morgan and the comedian W. C. Fields are among those reported to have had it, and a nose of this kind was used as a villain trait in the 1937 film Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs [1].

Rosacea is classed into erythematotelangiectatic, papulopustular, phymatous and ocular subtypes. Estimates of its prevalence range from 1 to 10 percent of people, with onset typically between ages 30 and 50, and it is not curable but is usually improved by treatment [4].

Rhinophyma involves thickening and irregular enlargement of nasal skin, concentrated at the nasal tip and alae, with prominent pores and a nodular surface. Histologically there is hyperplasia of sebaceous glands and fibrosis of connective tissue, and the underlying bone is not involved [1][2]. A clinicopathologic study described the spectrum of tissue changes seen in the condition [8].

It tends to develop gradually after years of rosacea. Rosacea usually begins with flushing, followed by persistent redness and visible vessels, then papules and pustules; a subset of people with inflammatory rosacea go on to develop tissue overgrowth [1]. Why only some progress is unknown, but a combination of neurovascular and immune disturbance is thought to be involved, and androgenic factors have been proposed to explain why men are affected far more often than women [1]. Wikipedia reports that the condition can be classified clinically into five grades of increasing severity, while Grokipedia describes alternative scales that rate it from minor to major based on thickening, lobulation and distortion [1][2].

Severe thickening can narrow the nasal airway and impair breathing, and the altered appearance can cause distress because observers may assume heavy drinking [1][2]. Grokipedia also describes chronic mouth breathing and, in some patients, anxiety and reduced quality of life linked to self-consciousness about the nose [2].

Medical sources describe two parallel tracks. Underlying rosacea is managed with topical or oral therapies intended to limit progression, while established rhinophyma generally needs removal of excess tissue [2][3][7]. A broad rosacea overview in the European dermatology literature notes that the condition has no cure and that management aims to suppress inflammatory lesions and redness [9]. Surgical options include tangential excision with a blade, electrosurgery, dermabrasion and ablative CO2 laser, sometimes combined [1][2].

Wikipedia describes the standard approach as paring down the bulk of tissue with a sharp instrument or laser and letting the area re-epithelialise, with complete excision and skin grafting reserved for some cases [1].

The use of the carbon dioxide laser to remove rhinophyma was described in a preliminary report in 1980 [5]. Clinicians describe the laser as sculpting away thickened tissue while leaving deeper glandular remnants from which new skin regrows [2][3]. Grokipedia reports sustained benefit in some cohorts over five years, though it does not substitute for the primary studies [2].

Because the lesion can mimic or conceal other diseases, sources state that pathological confirmation is advisable. Differential diagnoses include basal cell carcinoma, sarcoidosis, lymphoma and, in endemic regions, leishmaniasis [1][2]. Grokipedia gives an estimated 3 to 10 percent incidence of basal cell carcinoma within rhinophymatous tissue [2].

Tangential excision with a blade (sometimes called a rhinoshave) removes bulk layer by layer, with healing from the deep glandular remnants. Pooled data in the 2026 meta-analysis found scalpel excision to be the most common treatment (49.0 percent of treated patients), followed by CO2 laser (37.4 percent) [6]. A German study of 45 people combined a classic rhinoshave for coarse removal with fractional CO2 laser for fine contouring, followed patients for a median of 51 months, and reported a recurrence rate of 17.9 percent and one postoperative haemorrhage [6]. In a few severe cases the tissue is excised completely and covered with a skin graft [1].

Ablative CO2 laser removes the surplus tissue by vaporisation, with good control of bleeding. The 1980 preliminary report on four patients found satisfactory cosmetic results, excellent haemostasis and minimal morbidity, with complete healing in three to four weeks, similar to conventional methods [6]. A 2009 retrospective review from one centre covered 124 patients treated between 1996 and 2008 under local anaesthesia with continuous mode for debulking and a resurfacing or defocused mode for contouring; 115 completed treatment in one session, 118 had good to excellent results at three months, and complications included scarring and low pigment in four patients and open pores in two [6].

A 2025 retrospective cohort at a McGill-affiliated clinic followed 152 people with grade I to III rhinophyma for up to 12 months: 84 percent had significant aesthetic improvement, recurrence was 4 percent, and mild hypopigmentation occurred in 9 percent [6]. A Swedish series of 11 men with moderate to major rhinophyma reported 92 percent high satisfaction and 55 percent improved nasal airflow, with caution advised for darker skin types, and an Israeli series of 16 people reported very good or excellent aesthetic results in 81 percent [6]. A US case series of seven patients with melanated skin reported significant improvement in appearance and nasal obstruction, scarring in the nasal tip region in three, and suggested a more conservative resection depth may limit scarring [6].

Case reports and small series describe electrosurgical tangential decortication, electrosurgery combined with trichloroacetic acid application (six men, mean time to re-epithelialisation of 24 days), hydrosurgery, blue laser, and hyperbaric oxygen in reconstruction of giant rhinophyma; titles in the recent literature also include a combined rhinoplasty and rhinophyma approach and a case of triple relapse [6][6]. A 2008 review of treatment options in Annals of Plastic Surgery concluded that surgical removal of the hyperplastic tissue is the treatment of choice [6].

Reported outcomes in the series above include both appearance and function. Patients and surgeons describe the aim as reducing bulk at the nasal tip and alae, restoring a smoother surface with finer pores, and clearing a blocked airway; the Swedish series recorded improved airflow in 55 percent and the US series functional improvement in nasal obstruction [6]. Wikipedia lists psychological distress and stigma, including the assumed link to alcoholism, among the burdens of the condition [1].

Because rhinophyma develops in a subset of people with long-standing rosacea, treatment often continues for the underlying disease. A 2015 Cochrane review of 106 studies with 13,631 participants found high-quality evidence that topical ivermectin, azelaic acid and brimonidine, oral doxycycline and low-dose isotretinoin were more effective than placebo or comparators for moderate to severe rosacea, with most adverse events mild and transient [6]. Wikipedia notes that rosacea is not curable and lists triggers including sun, temperature extremes, alcohol, hot drinks and spicy food [4]. These therapies target inflammation; reviews describe established tissue overgrowth as generally needing procedural removal [2][3][7].

Reported satisfaction is generally high across series, but data are retrospective and use different follow-up periods and scoring. Recurrence figures reported include 4 percent in the 152-patient cohort and 17.9 percent in the German combined-technique study, while other series do not report it; a 2026 meta-analysis authors call for standardised treatment plans because methods and adverse effects vary [6]. A 2025 predictive modelling analysis in the 152-patient cohort identified grade, age and skin phototype as factors associated with outcomes such as hypopigmentation and satisfaction [6].

The 2026 systematic review pooled 149 case reports, case series and observational studies with 2,720 patients: men made up 58.9 percent, the mean age was 62.9 years, 61 percent had severe disease and 55.8 percent had rosacea documented [6]. Wikipedia and Grokipedia describe men as five to thirty times more likely than women to be affected, and the condition as rare in people of predominantly Asian or African ancestry in the United States [1][2].

Reviews and encyclopedic sources report that thickened nasal skin heals slowly and may scar, that secondary infection can occur in fissured tissue, and that a minority of lesions contain basal cell carcinoma or, more rarely, squamous cell carcinoma [2][3]. Recurrence is described as uncommon but possible, and regrowth is monitored [2].

A preliminary report from 1980 described removal of rhinophyma with the carbon dioxide laser [5]. A plastic-surgery review from 2002 summarised the clinical features, associated diagnoses and the surgical and non-surgical therapies, and set out an integrated treatment plan [3]. The clinicopathologic study mentioned above examined the histological variety of the condition [8].

Research on earlier rosacea stages is more extensive. A 1993 case-control study using standardized skin-surface biopsy of 49 people with rosacea and 45 controls found higher Demodex folliculorum density in rosacea [10]. A randomized double-blind trial in 63 people with papulopustular rosacea compared permethrin 5% cream, metronidazole 0.75% gel and placebo, scoring erythema, telangiectasia, edema, rhinophyma and mite counts [11]. These studies concern the inflammatory stages rather than surgical removal of rhinophyma. A 2022 review summarises current rosacea management [7].

The enlarged nose has long carried a cultural association with alcoholism, which has contributed to stigma for people with the condition [1]. Wikipedia notes that villainous characters in film have been shown with rhinophyma, including the disguised queen in Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, and that the banker J. P. Morgan and the comedian W. C. Fields were among those known to have had it before modern treatment [1].

The procedure is listed in this wiki because it is a nose-focused intervention that exists in the medical literature and is sometimes mentioned in discussions of hard and surgical looksmaxxing. It is a treatment for a disease rather than a routine cosmetic enhancement, and no published study evaluates it as a looksmaxxing intervention.

lore.intro: Rhinophyma appears in looksmaxxing discussion mainly as a medical nose procedure; no forum threads about it specifically were found, so the claims below record general beliefs about the condition and its treatment.
